title: Why Do Screens and Lights Flicker on Camera?
pause_note: long: beats listed in 'long' get a 1.5 s pause

beats: Film a lamp or a screen with your phone, and sometimes you see this.
Dark stripes, rolling through the picture.
Yet to your own eyes, the light looks perfectly steady.
So which one is telling the truth?
Both of them. And the reason starts in your wall socket.
The power in your wall is alternating current.
In Vietnam and Europe, it swings back and forth fifty times a second. In the United States, sixty.
Each swing has a push one way, and a push the other way.
A light does not care which way the current flows. It is bright at both peaks.
So it can peak twice per swing: a hundred, or a hundred and twenty times a second.
An old filament bulb stays hot between peaks, so it barely dims.
An LED has no such memory. It follows its power almost instantly. When the power dips, the light dips too.
A good LED driver smooths the power, and the light stays steady.
A cheap driver smooths it less, so the light can ripple, sometimes almost to dark.
Dimming adds another trick, called pulse width modulation.
The LED switches fully on and off, very fast, and stays off longer to look dimmer.
Many phone screens, and some laptop screens, dim this way at low brightness.
So why do you not see any of this?
Your eyes and brain add up light over a short moment, and blend fast changes into one glow.
For most people, flicker faster than about eighty times a second looks steady.
Some people still notice it, especially on dimmed screens, or when their eyes dart across a light.
A phone camera works differently.
Most phone cameras do not take the whole picture at once.
They read the sensor one row at a time, from top to bottom. This is called a rolling shutter.
Each row collects light for a very short moment, especially in bright scenes.
Rows caught at a peak come out bright. Rows caught in a dip come out dark.
Stack the rows, and the flicker becomes stripes across the picture.
Your eyes never see them, because they never look one row at a time.
But why do the stripes move?
Say your light pulses a hundred times a second, and your camera records thirty frames a second.
That is three and a third pulses per frame. That leftover third is the whole story.
So each new frame starts a third of a pulse later in the light's rhythm, and the stripes shift.
Frame after frame, they roll, like the wheels that seem to spin backwards on camera.
Now try a hundred and twenty pulses at thirty frames. That is exactly four per frame, so the stripes almost stand still.
The fix is to let every row collect whole pulses.
Use a pro camera mode. Where the power is fifty hertz, set the shutter to one fiftieth or one hundredth of a second.
Where it is sixty hertz, use one sixtieth or one hundred and twentieth.
Now every row gets the same amount of light, and the stripes fade away.
Many phones try to do this on their own, with a setting called anti banding.
So the stripes are not a fault in your camera.
They are the light's real rhythm, the one your eyes smooth over.
Point your phone at your lights tonight, and see which ones pulse.
